title: Feature flags & remote config
scopeHtml: Scope: flag architecture, Firebase Remote Config and alternatives, rollout/targeting, experiments, testing, multi-module placement, offline behavior, security and lifecycle for Android apps.

questions.promptHtml: What is a feature flag, what kinds of flags exist, and why do they matter on Android specifically, where you cannot redeploy instantly?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Checks whether you know flags are a delivery-risk tool, not an if statement, and that different flag kinds have different lifecycles.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: A feature flag is a runtime switch, controlled outside the binary, that decides which code path runs. On Android a release takes hours to days to reach users and cannot be pulled back, so flags decouple deploy from release: I ship code dark, turn it on gradually, and turn it off in minutes if it misbehaves. I separate four kinds: release flags (temporary), kill switches (long-lived, default-safe), experiment flags (temporary, tied to metrics) and permission/entitlement flags (permanent, business rules).

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
A Play Store rollout is slow: even with a staged rollout, adoption of a new version takes days, and a bad build cannot be recalled from devices that already updated. A server-controlled flag changes behavior of code already on the device.

             lifetime     default        owner        removal
release      weeks        OFF            feature team delete after 100% + soak
kill switch  years        ON (feature)   on-call/SRE  keep, test regularly
experiment   2-6 weeks    control        product/DS   delete after decision
entitlement  permanent    from backend   backend      not a flag; model as data

Mixing kinds is the root of flag debt: a release flag that stays forever becomes an undocumented permanent branch, while an entitlement (paid plan) modelled as a flag gets deleted by a cleanup sweep. Architecture: code never reads Remote Config directly; it asks a typed FeatureFlags API (see Q288), which hides the vendor, default values and caching.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
// Broken: stringly-typed vendor call scattered in UI code, no default policy
if (Firebase.remoteConfig.getBoolean("new_checkout")) showNewCheckout()

// Better: typed, central, defaulted
if (flags.isEnabled(Flag.NewCheckout)) showNewCheckout()

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Treating every flag as permanent "config"; nobody ever deletes them.
  • Using a flag to hide a security fix or an incomplete DB migration that is not actually safe when off.
  • Assuming the flag is instantly consistent across devices; it is eventually consistent.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Flag vs build variant? → Flavors are compile-time and need a release; flags are runtime. Use flavors for things that change the binary (permissions, SDKs), flags for behavior.
  2. Flag vs staged rollout in Play Console? → Play rollout controls who gets the binary; a flag controls what that binary does, and can be reverted without a new binary.
  3. Why not just ship behind a branch and merge when ready? → Long-lived branches cause merge pain and delay integration; trunk-based development with dark code keeps main shippable.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE: "turn features on/off remotely." Senior: classifies flags by lifecycle and owner, names the safe default for each, and ties flags to the release process (trunk-based, staged rollout, kill switch for risky paths).

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: Teams routinely discover a "temporary" release flag from two years ago is now load-bearing, because the off-path was never tested after refactors.

questions.promptHtml: How would you structure flag access in an Android codebase so that you can swap Firebase Remote Config for another vendor and always have a safe default?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Tests abstraction of a vendor SDK, defaults design, and typed API thinking.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: I define a small FlagProvider interface (read-only, synchronous reads from a local snapshot) and a typed Flag<T> definition that carries key and a compiled-in default. The Firebase implementation is one adapter. Reads never block on the network: they return the cached/activated value or the default. Fetching happens elsewhere, on a schedule or event.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Separate three concerns: definition (key, type, default, owner, expiry), provider (where values come from), and evaluation (precedence: local override > kill switch > remote value > default). Synchronous reads from an in-memory snapshot are essential: flag checks happen on the main thread in onCreate or Compose recomposition and must be cheap and non-suspending. Fetching is async and publishes a new snapshot.

Flag<T>(key, default) --> FlagProvider.get(flag) --> snapshot (memory)
                                  ^
        FirebaseProvider / OpenFeature / Debug override layer

OpenFeature (the CNCF vendor-neutral flag API, with a Kotlin SDK; verify current version) offers this abstraction ready-made, including evaluation context, if you want a standard instead of a house interface.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
class Flag<T : Any>(val key: String, val default: T, val owner: String)

object Flags {
    val NewCheckout = Flag("new_checkout", false, owner = "payments")
    val MaxUploadMb = Flag("max_upload_mb", 25L, owner = "media")
}

interface FlagProvider {
    fun <T : Any> get(flag: Flag<T>): T          // never blocks, never throws
}

class RemoteConfigProvider(private val rc: FirebaseRemoteConfig) : FlagProvider {
    @Suppress("UNCHECKED_CAST")
    override fun <T : Any> get(flag: Flag<T>): T = try {
        when (flag.default) {
            is Boolean -> rc.getBoolean(flag.key) as T
            is Long -> rc.getLong(flag.key) as T
            is String -> rc.getString(flag.key) as T
            else -> flag.default
        }
    } catch (e: Exception) { flag.default }
}

Note: Remote Config returns false/0/"" for a key that has neither a remote nor an in-app default, which silently equals "off" even for a flag whose safe default is on. Register in-app defaults via setDefaultsAsync from the same Flag list so they cannot drift.

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Default value duplicated at each call site and different in two places.
  • A suspend read API that forces every flag check into a coroutine.
  • Letting the vendor type (FirebaseRemoteConfigValue) leak into feature modules.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Where does the default come from if the key was never fetched? → The in-app default (setDefaultsAsync/the Flag default), and that default must be the safe behavior.
  2. Should flags be a Flow? → Expose a snapshot read plus an optional Flow for the few screens that must react live; most should read once at screen start.
  3. How do local debug overrides fit? → A provider decorator placed first in the chain, compiled only into debug builds.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE wraps getBoolean. Senior designs typed flags with owner and default in one place, non-blocking reads, a precedence chain and a debug override layer.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A flag whose in-app default was false while the intent was "on unless killed" meant every offline first-launch user lost a core feature.

questions.promptHtml: Explain how Firebase Remote Config fetch and activate work, including the minimum fetch interval, throttling, and real-time updates. When does a new value actually take effect?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Most flag incidents come from misunderstanding when a value becomes visible.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: Fetch downloads values into a staging area; activate makes them the values the app reads. fetchAndActivate() does both. Fetches are throttled by minimumFetchIntervalInSeconds, whose default is 12 hours per the SDK reference, so calling fetch more often just serves cached values and can end throttled. There is also a real-time listener (addOnConfigUpdateListener, SDK 21.3.0+ / BoM 31.2.4+) which pushes a notice, fetches the new template and lets you activate in onUpdate.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Three states exist per value: in-app default, last-fetched (staged), active. Reads see only active. Typical timing choices:

App start: fetchAndActivate() -> active values change mid-session (UI may flip)
App start: fetch(), activate on NEXT cold start -> consistent session, 1-launch lag
Real-time: listener -> fetch -> activate in onUpdate (still decide WHEN to apply)

Activating mid-session can change a flag between two reads in the same screen (see Q293). Many teams fetch early and activate at a safe boundary (next launch or next screen). The 12 hour default protects the backend and client quota; during development set the interval to 0 (the Firebase blog says to restore it before shipping). In production, hammering fetch does not make flags faster; the fetch call is throttled client-side and the status shows LAST_FETCH_STATUS_THROTTLED. Real-time updates avoid the polling-interval wait for kill switches; verify its behavior on your SDK version and note that it needs a persistent connection and does not work if the device is offline or the process is dead.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
val rc = Firebase.remoteConfig
rc.setConfigSettingsAsync(remoteConfigSettings { minimumFetchIntervalInSeconds = 3600 })
rc.setDefaultsAsync(R.xml.remote_config_defaults)

// start of process: fetch for next time, do not disturb the running session
rc.fetch().addOnCompleteListener { /* activate on next launch */ }

val reg = rc.addOnConfigUpdateListener(object : ConfigUpdateListener {
    override fun onUpdate(update: ConfigUpdate) {
        if ("kill_video" in update.updatedKeys) rc.activate()   // apply kill switches immediately
    }
    override fun onError(error: FirebaseRemoteConfigException) { /* keep last good */ }
})
// reg.remove() when no longer needed

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Calling fetch(0) in production, hitting throttling and wasting quota.
  • Reading flags before the first activate and caching the default forever in a singleton.
  • Assuming a fetch failure leaves you with no values; it keeps the last active ones.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Why does my new Remote Config value not show up on test devices? → Interval not elapsed, fetched but not activated, or condition targeting not matching; set interval 0 on debug.
  2. Which flags should apply immediately vs next launch? → Kill switches immediately; layout/behavior-changing flags at a boundary.
  3. How would you add a fast-path for emergencies beyond the 12 h default? → Real-time listener plus a lower interval for a dedicated kill-switch config, and push (FCM) as a nudge; verify limits.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE says "fetchAndActivate on launch." Senior picks activation timing per flag class and knows the cost of mid-session flips and throttling.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A kill switch took effect on only a fraction of users for half a day because most were inside the 12 h window.

questions.promptHtml: How does a percentage rollout work on the client, and how do you make it stable per user? What targeting dimensions would you support and what are the risks?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Tests understanding of deterministic bucketing and the difference between server-side and client-side evaluation.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: Hash a stable identifier together with the flag key (as salt) into a bucket 0-99 and compare it to the rollout percent. This is deterministic, so a user stays in the same group across sessions, and raising 5% to 20% only adds users. Salting per flag prevents the same users being in every experiment's first 5%. Targeting (country, app version, OS, device class) narrows who is eligible before the bucket check.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Evaluation can be server-side (SDK sends context, gets back the decided value; Firebase Remote Config conditions and percentile targeting work this way) or client-side (the client gets rules and evaluates them). Server evaluation keeps rules private; client evaluation works offline once rules are cached but exposes rules.

bucket = hash(flagKey + ":" + stableId) mod 100
enabled = eligible(context) && bucket < percent

Identifier choice: a logged-in user id gives cross-device consistency; an app-install id (Firebase installation id) is stable per install but resets on reinstall or clearing data, so a user can re-roll into the feature. Never use the advertising id. Use a good non-cryptographic hash such as Murmur3 (verify availability in your dependency), not String.hashCode() modulo, which has poor distribution on similar ids.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
fun bucket(flagKey: String, stableId: String): Int {
    val h = java.security.MessageDigest.getInstance("SHA-256")
        .digest("$flagKey:$stableId".toByteArray())
    val n = ((h[0].toInt() and 0xFF) shl 8) or (h[1].toInt() and 0xFF)  // 0..65535
    return n % 100
}
fun inRollout(flagKey: String, id: String, percent: Int) = bucket(flagKey, id) < percent

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Random.nextInt(100) per launch: users flicker in and out of the feature.
  • Reducing rollout then raising it again: users get re-exposed to a half-broken state; prefer kill and fix.
  • Targeting on app version with an off-by-one on semantic version comparison ("10.0" < "9.0" as strings).

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Why salt by flag key? → Otherwise the same 5% of users are guinea pigs for everything.
  2. Rollback at 20%? → Set to 0 or kill; bucket stability means no one flips unpredictably.
  3. Targeting 'internal staff first'? → A user-property/allowlist condition evaluated before percentage, plus a dogfood build with overrides.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE: "random percentage." Senior: deterministic salted hashing, stable-id tradeoffs (user vs install), and where evaluation runs and what that leaks.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: An install-id bucketed rollout re-enrolled users after "clear data" and polluted experiment results.

questions.promptHtml: In a multi-module Android app, where do flag definitions, the provider and the flag checks live? How do you avoid every module depending on Firebase?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Checks dependency direction and DI design applied to a cross-cutting concern.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: A tiny :core:flags API module holds Flag<T> and the FlagProvider interface and has no vendor dependency. The Firebase implementation lives in an :impl/app-level module bound through Hilt. Each feature module owns its own flag definitions and takes FlagProvider by injection; a feature does not read another feature's flags directly.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Putting all flag keys into one central Flags object in :core makes every feature change touch a shared module (build invalidation, merge conflicts) and encourages cross-feature coupling. Better: API module is generic; each feature declares internal object CheckoutFlags in its own module. A registry for the debug menu is assembled with Hilt multibindings (@IntoSet) so the app can list all flags without a central file.

:core:flags (api)         Flag<T>, FlagProvider
:core:flags-firebase      RemoteConfigProvider  (only app depends on it)
:feature:checkout         CheckoutFlags + uses FlagProvider
:app                      Hilt binds FlagProvider -> RemoteConfigProvider

Feature modules depending on the interface keeps them testable with a fake and keeps Firebase out of their classpath (faster builds, easier KMP later).

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
// :feature:checkout
internal object CheckoutFlags { val NewPay = Flag("checkout_new_pay", false, "payments") }

class CheckoutViewModel @Inject constructor(private val flags: FlagProvider) : ViewModel() {
    val useNewPay = flags.get(CheckoutFlags.NewPay)   // read once, stable for this screen
}

// :app
@Module @InstallIn(SingletonComponent::class)
abstract class FlagModule { @Binds abstract fun provider(i: RemoteConfigProvider): FlagProvider }

@Module @InstallIn(SingletonComponent::class)
object CheckoutFlagRegistry { @Provides @IntoSet fun flags(): Flag<*> = CheckoutFlags.NewPay }

Because CheckoutFlags is internal, the registry module must live in the same module (put the @Provides @IntoSet there); the snippet is illustrative.

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Feature module A reading new_checkout to alter its own behavior based on feature B's flag.
  • A flag check deep inside a library module with no way to inject.
  • One giant Flags object recompiling every module on each new flag.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. How does the debug menu list all flags? → Hilt multibinding set of Flag<*> contributed by each module.
  2. Flag controls navigation to a feature module? → Check at the navigation entry point in the app/host module, not inside the feature.
  3. Dynamic feature modules? → The flag only decides entry; the install itself is separate (see the dynamic feature chunk).

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE keeps one global singleton. Senior makes the API module vendor-free, scopes flag ownership per feature, and uses DI multibindings for discovery.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: One shared flags file in :core caused near-daily merge conflicts and full rebuilds on a 60-module project.

questions.promptHtml: How do you test code that sits behind feature flags, unit, UI and release-wise?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Flags double the state space; interviewers want to see how you control it.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: Inject the provider, use a FakeFlagProvider in unit and UI tests, and test both branches of every flag that is not yet removed. Never let tests hit the real Remote Config. For release safety, test the default configuration (all flags at their in-app defaults) because that is what an offline first-launch user sees, and test the kill-off state of every kill switch.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html: For N independent flags there are 2^N combinations; you cannot test all, so: (1) test each flag on and off in isolation with others at default; (2) test the "everything at ship default" combination; (3) for flags that interact, declare the dependency explicitly and test the pairs. Instrumented tests should set flags through the DI graph (Hilt @TestInstallIn replacing the provider module), not through the network. Screenshot tests can parametrize on flag state.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
class FakeFlagProvider(private val values: MutableMap<String, Any> = mutableMapOf()) : FlagProvider {
    fun set(flag: Flag<*>, v: Any) { values[flag.key] = v }
    @Suppress("UNCHECKED_CAST")
    override fun <T : Any> get(flag: Flag<T>): T = (values[flag.key] ?: flag.default) as T
}

@Test fun newPay_on_showsNewSheet() {
    val flags = FakeFlagProvider().apply { set(CheckoutFlags.NewPay, true) }
    val vm = CheckoutViewModel(flags)
    assertTrue(vm.useNewPay)
}

@TestInstallIn(components = [SingletonComponent::class], replaces = [FlagModule::class])
@Module abstract class FakeFlagModule { @Binds abstract fun p(f: FakeFlagProvider): FlagProvider }

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Only testing the "on" path while the "off" path (the production path today) rots.
  • Tests that depend on Remote Config network state: flaky.
  • Forgetting that removing a flag is itself a change needing the surviving path's tests to still pass.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. How do you catch a flag whose off-path is broken? → CI matrix running critical-path tests with all kill switches off and with all release flags at default.
  2. How do you test activation timing? → Provider fake that changes the snapshot mid-test and assert the screen does not flip.
  3. QA wants to test a prod flag state? → Debug-menu override layer plus a Remote Config condition for QA user ids.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE mocks the flag. Senior bounds the combinatorics, tests defaults and kill states, and automates cleanup so the matrix shrinks.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A kill switch's "off" path crashed because no test had run it since a refactor, so the emergency toggle caused the second incident.

questions.contextHtml:
A checkout screen with 2M DAU shows a "Pay" button that sometimes does nothing for about 0.3% of sessions. Crash-free is unaffected. Support logs show users who tapped Pay right after the app was foregrounded. The code:

class CheckoutFragment : Fragment() {
    override fun onViewCreated(v: View, s: Bundle?) {
        if (flags.get(CheckoutFlags.NewPay)) {
            payButton.setOnClickListener { newPayFlow.start() }
        } else {
            payButton.setOnClickListener { legacyPay.start() }
        }
    }
    override fun onResume() {
        super.onResume()
        remoteConfig.fetchAndActivate()
    }
    fun onTotalReady(t: Total) {
        summary.text = if (flags.get(CheckoutFlags.NewPay)) newFormat(t) else oldFormat(t)
        payButton.isEnabled = !flags.get(CheckoutFlags.NewPay) || t.hasToken
    }
}

A staged rollout of checkout_new_pay from 10% to 50% happened that afternoon.
questions.promptHtml: Find the bug and explain why it only hits some sessions.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Network race, add a loading state." Misses that the same flag is read at three moments and fetchAndActivate on every resume lets the value change between reads.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Does the broken session correlate with users in the newly enrolled 10-50% band? Does the problem appear after a resume? Is hasToken tied to the new flow only? These split flag-flip from data bugs.
  2. Immediate mitigation: Set the flag back to 10%; flip-flop sessions fall as fewer users are near the boundary. Stop activating on resume via a hotfix flag if available.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) Mid-screen flag flip: onViewCreated bound the legacy click listener, then onResume activation switched the flag to on, so onTotalReady sees on and disables the button until a token that the legacy path never fetches. (b) A race in token fetch (red herring: the 10% to 50% timing points elsewhere). (c) Process death restore reading a different flag value than before.
  4. How I'd verify each: Log the flag value at each read with a session id; reproduce with a fake provider that flips after onViewCreated; check enrollment timing vs affected sessions in analytics; a unit test asserting a single read.
  5. Root cause: The flag is read three times with no snapshot, and activation happens mid-session. State derived from the flag in onViewCreated disagrees with state in onTotalReady.
  6. Fix: Short-term: read once into a val in the ViewModel and use that value everywhere on the screen; activate at next launch. Long-term: provider exposes an immutable per-session snapshot; activation only at process start (kill switches excepted, and those take effect on the next screen).
class CheckoutViewModel @Inject constructor(flags: FlagProvider) : ViewModel() {
    val newPay = flags.get(CheckoutFlags.NewPay)   // frozen for this VM's lifetime
}
  1. Prevention: Lint/detekt rule banning fetchAndActivate outside the flag module; test that flips the fake mid-screen; log "flag exposure" once per session.
  2. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: I would not remove runtime updates altogether since kill switches need them; I would not add synchronized or debounce, which hides the flip rather than preventing it.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• What if the flag must update live for a kill switch? → Apply at a navigation boundary and show the legacy path on the next screen entry.
  • Two flags interact? → Read both into one immutable CheckoutConfig object at screen start.
  • Process death and restore? → Persist the decision in SavedStateHandle so the restored screen matches.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A pay screen flipped paths between onViewCreated and a data callback after a resume-time activate. A single frozen read in the ViewModel fixed it, and the incident became a rule: one read per screen.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: Blames networking, adds spinners.
  • Hire: Finds the multiple reads and the mid-session activate and freezes the value.
  • Strong hire: Also proposes session snapshots, activation boundary policy, lint rule and process-death handling.

questions.contextHtml: A video feature rolled out to 100% in v8.4 (5M DAU, 60% on v8.4). At 14:05 crash-free drops from 99.7% to 97.1%; stack: java.lang.IllegalStateException: MediaCodec ... on Android 12 Samsung devices. At 14:12 you set the Remote Config key video_v2_enabled=false. At 16:00 the crash rate is still 2.4%. Dashboards show only ~35% of crashing devices fetching the new value. The app uses minimumFetchIntervalInSeconds = 43200 and fetches only on cold start. A teammate suggests a hotfix release. Another notes the default in code is true.
questions.promptHtml: What is happening, and what do you do now and next?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Wait for propagation" or "ship a hotfix". Both miss that the kill switch design itself is failing and ignore faster levers.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: What fraction of crashing sessions are long-lived (not cold-started since 14:12)? What is the fetch interval and where is fetch called? Is a real-time listener wired? Can the backend refuse the feature server-side? Each tells me which lever exists.
  2. Immediate mitigation: Roll the Play staged rollout back/halt it (stop new installs of v8.4), and disable the feature server-side if the video session needs a backend token (backend returns "unavailable"). Push a high-priority FCM data message that triggers fetch for v8.4 users. The Remote Config change stays.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) Interval: 12 hour default style intervals plus cold-start-only fetch means many users have not refetched. (b) Fetch happens but activation deferred to next launch. (c) The true in-app default re-enables when fetch fails or cache is cleared. (d) Crash cause unrelated to the flag (red herring, but check the exposure correlation).
  4. How I'd verify each: Firebase console fetch metrics and a custom event flag_fetch_ok/flag_active_value; crash reports tagged with the flag value as a custom key; split crash rate by flag value; throttling status logs.
  5. Root cause: The kill switch had the same propagation path as an ordinary release flag: long interval, cold-start fetch, deferred activation, and an unsafe default (true).
  6. Fix: Short-term as above. Long-term: a dedicated kill-switch channel: real-time listener plus short interval on a small config, activation immediate, default off for risky features, and a server-side gate.
rc.addOnConfigUpdateListener(object : ConfigUpdateListener {
    override fun onUpdate(u: ConfigUpdate) {
        if (u.updatedKeys.any { it.startsWith("kill_") }) rc.activate()
    }
    override fun onError(e: FirebaseRemoteConfigException) {}
})
  1. Prevention: Game-day: flip each kill switch in staging and measure time to 95% of active devices; set flag_value crash keys; alert on "kill executed but exposure still above X after 30 min".
  2. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Not a hotfix first: it takes a review cycle plus adoption days and the crash persists on old builds anyway. Not set the interval to 0 globally, which gets throttled and burns quota.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Users offline? → Cannot be reached; the crash must be survivable client-side (catch the MediaCodec failure and fall back, a crash-loop circuit breaker).
  • Crash at startup so the app never fetches? → Crash-loop detection: after 3 crashes within N minutes, force the safe defaults locally and skip the feature.
  • Why not default false for everything? → Release flags yes; for long-shipped features a false default silently disables them offline, so defaults are per class.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A kill switch "worked" in staging with a debug interval of 0 but took most of a day in production. Afterward, every kill switch's time-to-effect was measured in a rehearsal, and a client-side crash-loop breaker was added.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: Waits for propagation or only hotfixes.
  • Hire: Diagnoses interval/activation, uses FCM nudge and Play halt.
  • Strong hire: Redesigns the kill channel, adds crash-loop breaker, measures time-to-effect, defaults per class.

questions.promptHtml: You are asked to plumb A/B experiments through the app. What does the client need to do correctly beyond reading a flag, and what commonly invalidates results?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Separates people who treat experiments as "if variant == B" from people who understand assignment, exposure and analysis hygiene.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: The client must get a stable assignment, apply it consistently, and log an exposure event at the moment the user actually sees the treatment, not at fetch time. Without correct exposure logging and stable assignment, the analysis is biased: too many users counted, users switching groups, or mismatched denominators (sample ratio mismatch).

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Assignment is ideally decided server-side or by a deterministic hash (Q290) and delivered as part of the config. Firebase A/B Testing runs on Remote Config and Analytics; alternatives include Statsig, LaunchDarkly, Optimizely, GrowthBook (verify feature sets). Client responsibilities:

assign (stable) -> apply (once per session) -> log exposure (when rendered) -> log metrics with variant

Pitfalls:

  • Exposure logged at app start for users who never reach the screen dilutes the effect (a diluted analysis includes non-exposed users).
  • Late activation: a user gets control for the first launch (default) then treatment later, contaminating groups; define "first-launch" policy (wait briefly for fetch, then proceed with default and exclude from the experiment).
  • Sample ratio mismatch: observed 52/48 on a 50/50 split signals a bug such as crashes in one arm or exposure logging failing for one arm.
  • Crash/ANR/startup time are guardrail metrics and must carry the variant.
  • Interaction between concurrent experiments on the same screen.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
class ExperimentClient(private val flags: FlagProvider, private val analytics: Analytics) {
    private val exposed = mutableSetOf<String>()
    fun variant(exp: Flag<String>): String = flags.get(exp)   // frozen per session
    fun logExposure(exp: Flag<String>) {
        if (exposed.add(exp.key)) analytics.log("exposure", mapOf("exp" to exp.key, "variant" to variant(exp)))
    }
}
// Call logExposure(Exp.Onboarding) in onResume of the screen that renders the variant.

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Logging exposure for both arms in different places so counts are asymmetric.
  • Using Remote Config values as the source of truth without attaching the variant to crash keys.
  • Peeking and stopping early.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. How to avoid network-delay bias on cold start? → Short bounded wait or persisted assignment from the last launch; users without assignment are excluded.
  2. Sample ratio mismatch cause on Android? → One arm crashes more (loses events), or the new view logs differently; check logs per arm.
  3. Same user on two devices? → Needs a user-id-based assignment, not install-id.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE: branch on variant. Senior: stable assignment, exposure-at-render, guardrails, SRM checks and a consistency policy for first launch.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A "winning" variant turned out to be a logging bug: exposure fired only in the new layout.

questions.contextHtml: The app has 340 active flags across 70 modules after 4 years. A post-incident review found that a 2-year-old flag use_new_cache was set to false in a config cleanup, because the owner left. Cold-start p95 went from 1.8 s to 4.1 s for 12% of users within a day (the new cache is still the only supported implementation on the main path but the old one was kept as fallback). Build time rose 8% from dead branches. PMs ship about 25 flags a quarter, and nobody is assigned to remove them.
questions.promptHtml: Design the process and tooling so this does not recur, and how do you pay down the existing 340.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Add a comment to remove later" or "ban flags". Doesn't address ownership, classification and automation.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Which of the 340 are fully on/off for 100% for 90+ days? Which are permanent entitlements? Do we have a flag registry with owners? What deletion tools can we use (Piranha-like codemods, manual)?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Restore use_new_cache to true; lock the key (require review for any change to flags older than N days); add alerting on cold-start p95 by flag value.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: Process failure (no owner/expiry), classification failure (release vs permanent), and tooling failure (no automated stale detection).
  4. How I'd verify each: Export flag values and last-change times from the console; compute per-flag exposure counts from analytics; grep code for each key; build-scan to see time attributable to dead branches.
  5. Root cause: Flags had no lifecycle metadata; a temporary release flag became a de facto permanent one and a dead fallback stayed reachable via config.
  6. Fix: Every Flag declaration requires owner, type and expires (a date) enforced by an annotation processor/lint rule. A weekly job lists flags at 100% for 30+ days or past expiry and opens a ticket to the owner's team; owners go to a team, not a person. Uber's Piranha (open source) automates deleting stale-flag code on Android/iOS via AST refactoring; for Kotlin consider a codemod or manual deletion PR template. Delete both the flag and the dead branch together.
class Flag<T : Any>(val key: String, val default: T, val owner: String,
                    val type: FlagType, val expires: String? /* ISO date, null for KILL/PERMANENT */)
// lint: error if type == RELEASE && expires == null, or expires < today
  1. Prevention: Flag budget per team, expiry lint in CI, dashboard of flag age, "delete" part of the feature's definition of done, quarterly cleanup sprint.
  2. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Not a mass delete: some "stale" flags are intentional kill switches (Uber notes this complicates automation), so classify first. Not rely on people remembering.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Flag removal in the same PR as 100% rollout? → No; soak first, then delete in a later release so a rollback is possible.
  • Server stopped sending the key, app still has it? → In-app default must equal the final shipped behavior before the server deletes the key.
  • Remove for old versions still in the field? → Keep the server key until the min supported version no longer reads it.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A cleanup of "unused" keys broke an old app version still reading them. After that, deleting a server-side key required a min-version check.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: Ad hoc cleanup, no ownership.
  • Hire: Owner/expiry metadata, CI enforcement, regular cleanup.
  • Strong hire: Classification, automation (codemods), safe key deletion with version support, metrics-based alerts.

questions.contextHtml: A fintech app (3M DAU) gates a premium "instant payout" feature with Remote Config key payout_instant_enabled and also keeps the fee in instant_fee_bps. A security review reports: (1) a rooted device with Frida can force the flag true and the button appears; (2) a user changed the fee value to 0 locally and the app displayed a 0% fee; (3) the Remote Config template contains an unreleased partner's name in a parameter description and a key named acme_exclusive_launch_q3. Server logs show 14 requests to the payout API from clients that displayed instant payout without eligibility.
questions.promptHtml: What is the right security model for flags, and what do you change?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Obfuscate the keys" or "use root detection". Treats the client as trusted.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Does the backend re-check eligibility? Does the server compute the fee? Are any secrets/PII in config? Is the Remote Config template readable by clients, which means all values and keys are visible?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Verify server rejects ineligible instant payouts and rate-limit; rename/purge sensitive key names from the template; confirm those 14 requests were rejected.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: The root issue is trust placement: client flags are UX hints only. Secondary: information disclosure via keys/values. Third: tampering with local cached values.
  4. How I'd verify each: Inspect the fetch response with a proxy to see what clients receive; try the exploit on a debug build; run API tests as an ineligible user; review template for secrets.
  5. Root cause: Authorization decisions and money values were derived from client-visible, client-modifiable config.
  6. Fix: The server owns entitlement and the fee: the payout endpoint verifies eligibility and computes the fee; the client displays what the server returned (GET /payout/options). Remote Config keeps only UX toggles (show/hide the entry). Keep secrets and unreleased details out of keys and descriptions; use neutral names.
// UI hint only; the server decides
val show = flags.get(PayoutFlags.ShowInstant) && options.instantAllowed
// payout request carries NO fee; the server computes and returns the quote id
api.confirm(quoteId = options.quoteId)
  1. Prevention: Security review checklist item "flag guards authorization?", API tests for each gated endpoint, template review in change management, access control on who edits Remote Config (it needs roles/audit).
  2. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Not rely on root detection/obfuscation as primary defense; it only raises cost. Server-side checks add a round trip but are the only trustworthy layer.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Can I sign the config? → Remote Config is delivered over TLS and you can pin; signing the values yourself helps against local tamper but not against a user who controls the whole app; server checks remain mandatory.
  • Is hiding unreleased feature names realistic? → Use opaque keys and ship the code dark; assume strings in the APK are readable anyway.
  • Server flags vs client flags? → Authorization and pricing flags live on the server; the client receives the resolved result.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A beta feature name leaked to the press from a public config template. After that, keys were opaque and entitlements moved server-side.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: Obfuscation/root detection only.
  • Hire: Server-side authorization, treats client flags as hints.
  • Strong hire: Also sanitizes template, access control/audit, API tests, quote-based fee design.

questions.promptHtml: How should an app behave on the first launch with no network, or when Remote Config fetch is slow or fails? Do you block startup on fetching flags?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Tests startup performance thinking, resilience and the cost of getting defaults wrong.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: I never block cold start on the network. The app starts immediately with last-known-good values persisted on disk (Remote Config persists activated values), and on a true first launch with no cache it uses bundled in-app defaults that are chosen to be the safe behavior. Fetch runs in the background with a timeout and the result is applied at a defined boundary. The only exception is a flag that gates something that cannot be shown wrongly (e.g., an experiment's first screen), where I allow a short bounded wait (for example 1-2 seconds, tuned from p95 fetch latency) then fall back.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Layers of value, highest precedence first: local override (debug) > active remote value > persisted last-known-good > compiled default. Remote Config handles the persistence and defaults, but you decide "safe". For each flag classify:

risky new feature     default OFF  (offline users get the old stable behavior)
kill-switchable old   default ON   (do not silently remove shipped features offline)
experiment            default control; mark user "unassigned" and exclude

Startup cost: do not call fetch on the main thread's critical path; start it after first frame or from an App Startup initializer with lazy semantics. Blocking on fetch adds the network RTT to time-to-first-render (a p95 on poor networks of seconds), which hurts retention more than most flag-gated features help. Also consider a server-mandated "minimum version"/maintenance gate as a separate concern.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
class FlagBootstrap @Inject constructor(private val rc: FirebaseRemoteConfig, @AppScope private val scope: CoroutineScope) {
    fun start() {
        rc.setDefaultsAsync(R.xml.remote_config_defaults)
        scope.launch {
            withTimeoutOrNull(5_000) { rc.fetch().await() }   // kotlinx-coroutines-play-services
            // activate at next launch or boundary; do not touch the running UI
        }
    }
}

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Splash screen waiting for fetchAndActivate: a fetch failure becomes a startup delay of the timeout every time.
  • Default false for long-shipped features so offline users lose them.
  • Treating "fetch failed" as an error to retry in a tight loop.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. How would you measure the cost of waiting? → Compare time-to-initial-display with and without the wait using Macrobenchmark and field startup metrics.
  2. First launch of an experiment? → Persist the assignment once fetched; exclude unassigned sessions.
  3. Remote Config returns stale values for weeks (device offline)? → Add a max-age: after N days with no successful fetch, drop risky flags to their safe default.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE blocks on fetch or uses false defaults everywhere. Senior classifies defaults, never blocks the critical path, adds max-age for stale caches and measures the startup impact.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A splash that awaited fetch added about 2 s to cold start on poor networks and measurably lowered day-1 retention until it was made async.
